title: Preface
summary: Apple Inc.’s Form 10-K cover page identifies its fiscal year ended September 25, 2021, California incorporation, headquarters, contact details, and SEC file number. It lists its common stock and debt securities registered on Nasdaq and no Section 12(g) securities. The filing confirms required reporting and interactive data submissions, large accelerated filer status, auditor attestation of internal controls, and that Apple is not a shell company. It reports approximately $2.021 trillion in nonaffiliate market value at March 26, 2021, and 16.406 billion shares outstanding October 15, 2021.

title: DOCUMENTS INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE
summary: Apple’s 2021 Form 10-K incorporates portions of its 2022 proxy statement into Part III and provides its contents across four parts, covering business, risks, financial results, governance, and exhibits. It explains forward-looking statements, their risks and identifying terms, and fiscal-year and Company terminology. The business overview describes Apple’s products and fiscal calendar, including 2020–2021 releases of iPhone, Mac, iPad, and Wearables, Home and Accessories, with their operating systems and key chip, connectivity, and product features.

title: Apple’s Business and 2021 Product Lines
summary: The page explains that the Form 10-K contains risk-bearing forward-looking statements, how to identify them, and that Apple need not update them except as required by law. It defines fiscal-period and Company terminology, then describes Apple’s business, fiscal year, and products: iPhone, Mac, iPad, and Wearables, Home and Accessories, including their operating systems and major releases from 2020–2021.

title: Apple Services, Markets, and Distribution
key_items: Advertising; AppleCare; Cloud Services; Digital Content; Payment Services
summary: Apple’s services include advertising through third-party licensing and its own platforms; fee-based AppleCare support, repairs, replacements, and, where available, additional damage or loss coverage; cloud storage and syncing across Apple devices and Windows PCs; platforms for downloading apps and digital content, plus subscriptions for games, music, news, video, and personalized fitness; and Apple Card and Apple Pay. Customers span consumer, business, education, enterprise, and government markets. Apple sells its own and third-party products through retail and online stores, direct sales, and indirect channels such as carriers, wholesalers, retailers, and resellers. In 2021, direct and indirect channels generated 36% and 64% of net sales, respectively.

title: Competition
summary: Apple faces intense competition marked by price pressure, rapid innovation, short product cycles, imitation and IP infringement. Success depends on timely innovation and factors including price, features, quality, design, ecosystem, distribution, support and reputation; rivals may have broader offerings, larger customer bases, lower costs, or free-content models. Component supply can be constrained by limited sources, shortages, price swings, custom-part capacity, and uncertain supply agreements; manufacturing is largely outsourced in Asia. Apple invests in R&D, licensing and acquisitions. It protects innovations through extensive global IP rights but also depends on personnel and third-party licenses, whose future availability and terms are uncertain.

title: Competition, Components, R&D and Intellectual Property
summary: The Company faces intense competition across its device and services markets, including price pressure, competitors with broader offerings and larger installed bases, free or illegitimate content models, and imitation or integration of features. Components may be limited to single sources, subject to shortages and price fluctuations, or constrained by custom manufacturing capacity; supply agreements may not be renewed, and most hardware is outsourced, primarily in Asia. Competitiveness depends on timely innovation, supported by R&D, licensing and acquisitions. The Company protects innovations through a broad portfolio of patents, copyrights, trademarks and other rights, but also relies on its people and third-party intellectual property licenses, which may not remain available on reasonable terms.

title: Business Seasonality and Human Capital
key_items: Workplace Practices and Policies; Compensation and Benefits; Growth and Development; Inclusion and Diversity; Engagement; Health and Safety
summary: The page describes seasonal and product-launch effects on sales, expenses, and channel inventory, and Apple’s workforce of about 154,000. It outlines commitments to a respectful, equitable workplace; competitive compensation and broad benefits; employee growth and education; inclusive hiring, representation, outreach, and employee groups; open communication and engagement surveys; and workplace risk prevention, safety training, and COVID-19 protections and support.

title: Available Information
summary: Apple files its annual, quarterly, current, and amended Exchange Act reports with the SEC, where they are available free through Apple’s investor relations website when posted by the SEC. Apple also shares investor information on its corporate and investor relations websites, including press releases, financial performance, environmental, social and governance matters, and annual shareholder meeting details. Website content is not incorporated into the Form 10-K, and URL references are inactive textual references.

title: Risk Factors and COVID-19 Impacts
key_items: The Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition, as well as the price of the Company’s stock, have been adversely affected and could in the future be materially adversely affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.
summary: The risk factors section warns that known or unknown risks can materially harm the Company’s business, reputation, results, financial condition, and stock price; past performance is not a reliable guide, and the discussion includes forward-looking statements and should be read with the related MD&A and financial statements. COVID-19 has disrupted economic activity, markets, suppliers, manufacturing, logistics, retail and partner sales, and work arrangements. Future effects remain uncertain and depend on factors including the pandemic’s course, variants, vaccines, public-health measures, the economy, and consumer demand. Potential impacts include reduced demand, supply-chain and sales-channel disruption, impaired strategy execution, and lower profitability; the pandemic may amplify other risks.

title: Macroeconomic and Industry Risks
key_items: The Company’s operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions and adverse economic conditions can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition.

The Company’s business can be impacted by political events, trade and other international disputes, war, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues, industrial accidents and other business interruptions.
Global markets for the Company’s products and services are highly competitive and subject to rapid technological change, and the Company may be unable to compete effectively in these markets.
summary: The text outlines Apple’s risks from global economic downturns, inflation, tariffs, policy and currency changes, weaker consumer spending, and financial instability among suppliers, partners, and financial institutions. Political disputes, trade restrictions, disasters, climate change, accidents, cyberattacks, labor issues, and pandemics may disrupt operations, supply chains, sales, and services; recovery can be costly, and insurance may be inadequate. It also describes intense global competition, rapid technological change, pricing pressure, short product cycles, uncertain R&D returns, intellectual-property infringement, and competitors’ scale and resources, all threatening Apple’s innovation, market position, margins, and financial results.

title: Business Risks

nodes.title: To remain competitive and stimulate customer demand, the Company must successfully manage frequent introductions and transitions of products and services.
nodes.summary: Apple faces business risks from the need to continually develop and launch new products, services, and technologies, improve existing offerings, drive customer demand, and manage transitions in volatile, competitive markets. Success depends on timely development and market acceptance; managing production ramp-ups, software availability, purchase commitments and inventory; supplying sufficient quantities at expected costs; and avoiding quality defects. Apple cannot guarantee successful future introductions or transitions.

nodes.title: Manufacturing and Component Supply Risks
key_items: The Company depends on component and product manufacturing and logistical services provided by outsourcing partners, many of which are located outside of the U.S.
Future operating results depend upon the Company’s ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms.
nodes.summary: The Company relies on concentrated, often single-source outsourcing partners—primarily in Asia—for components, manufacturing, assembly, and logistics. Reduced control, partner failures or misconduct, and disruptions from disasters, technical, economic, labor, health, political, or trade events can affect product quality, supply, delivery, costs, reputation, and financial results. Equipment held by partners and supplier prepayments may be at risk if partners face financial distress. Limited sources, shortages, price volatility, semiconductor constraints, supplier failures, and difficulty renewing supply agreements threaten component availability and commercially reasonable terms. Custom components for new products may face capacity constraints or discontinued supply; delays and difficulty securing alternative sources can materially harm results.

nodes.title: Product Quality, Asset and Intellectual Property Risks
key_items: The Company’s products and services may be affected from time to time by design and manufacturing defects that could materially adversely affect the Company’s business and result in harm to the Company’s reputation.
The Company is exposed to the risk of write-downs on the value of its inventory and other assets, in addition to purchase commitment cancellation risk.
The Company relies on access to third-party intellectual property, which may not be available to the Company on commercially reasonable terms or at all.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from design, manufacturing, component, software and service defects, including safety hazards, outages, liability, recalls, costs, lost sales and reputational damage. It covers inventory obsolescence, asset impairments and cancellation fees, as well as forecasting errors that may leave excess or insufficient inventory or unused purchase commitments. It also explains reliance on third-party intellectual property licenses, possible infringement claims, and the risk that licenses may be unavailable or commercially unreasonable, restricting sales and harming business results.

nodes.title: The Company’s future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers.
nodes.summary: The Company’s performance depends on third-party developers continuing to create and maintain appealing, compatible applications; its minority market share may steer developer resources to competitors, reducing app availability and quality. App Store business, commissions and distribution practices may change due to competition, legislation, litigation or investigations, potentially harming results. Digital-content licensing may become unavailable or costly, while in-house content is expensive, may not appeal, and faces pandemic-related production constraints; required security technology may also be costly or delayed. Success depends on retaining skilled employees and its culture, and on carriers, wholesalers, retailers and resellers; carrier financing, installment plans and subsidies may be reduced or discontinued.

nodes.title: Risks to Apps, Digital Content, and Talent
key_items: Failure to obtain or create digital content that appeals to the Company’s customers, or to make such content available on commercially reasonable terms, could have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition.
The Company’s success depends largely on the continued service and availability of highly skilled employees, including key personnel.
nodes.summary: The Company’s smaller market share may discourage developers, limiting the availability and quality of applications; rapid technology shifts can also leave apps outdated or malfunctioning. App Store competition, legal and regulatory changes, and litigation may alter distribution and commissions, reducing revenue. Third-party content access may be costly, limited, or short-term, while original content is expensive and may not appeal; production restrictions and changing security requirements add risks. Success also depends on retaining highly skilled employees and key leaders amid intense competition, supported by maintaining the Company’s culture.

nodes.title: The Company depends on the performance of carriers, wholesalers, retailers and other resellers.
nodes.summary: The Company relies on carriers and resellers, who also sell competitors’ products, and on carrier financing and subsidies that may change. Investments in reseller support may not generate returns, and reseller weakness or uncertainty may reduce distribution and promotion. IT failures and network disruptions affecting the Company or its supply chain can interrupt services, transactions, manufacturing and shipping despite continuity measures. Confidential information is shared internally and with third parties; breaches, cyberattacks and other disruptions may occur despite security investments, damage reputation and operations, deter customers, harm relationships, and lead to litigation, investigations, fines or financial losses. The Company faces elevated targeting risks, uses safeguards and customer protections that can themselves impede access or orders, and insurance may not cover all losses or claims.

nodes.title: Reseller Investment, IT Disruptions, and Data Security Risks
key_items: The Company’s business and reputation are impacted by information technology system failures and network disruptions.

Losses or unauthorized access to or releases of confidential information, including personal information, could subject the Company to significant reputational, financial, legal and operational consequences.
nodes.summary: Reseller sales programs require substantial investment without guaranteed returns, and reseller weakness or uncertain demand may reduce distribution, orders, and marketing. IT failures and network disruptions—from disasters, outages, or cyber incidents—could interrupt online services, transactions, manufacturing, and shipping despite continuity measures. Confidential information risks include breaches involving the Company or third parties, increasingly frequent and sophisticated attacks, and heightened targeting due to the Company’s profile. Security controls, customer protections, and insurance may be inadequate; incidents could harm operations, finances, reputation, customer and commercial relationships, stock price, and lead to litigation, investigations, fines, or penalties.

nodes.title: Risks of Investments and Retail Operations
key_items: Investment in new business strategies and acquisitions could disrupt the Company’s ongoing business, present risks not originally contemplated and adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations and financial condition.
The Company’s retail stores have required and will continue to require a substantial investment and commitment of resources and are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties.
nodes.summary: New strategies and acquisitions may distract management, create unexpected costs, liabilities, regulatory or operational challenges, fail to earn adequate returns, or require asset write-offs; transactions may face approval delays or restrictions, and unsuccessful ventures could harm the Company’s reputation and financial results. Retail stores require substantial investment, staffing, inventory, and lease commitments, especially high-profile locations. High costs make sales declines, poor performance, or closures potentially costly through lease termination, asset write-offs, and severance. Retail risks also include economic conditions, construction and operating costs, retail-partner relationships, inventory-value fluctuations, and securing or renewing affordable leases in quality locations.

summary: The section covers risks from sustaining innovation, product launches, transitions, demand, quality, supply and inventory management; dependence on concentrated suppliers and manufacturing partners, component availability, and disruption or financial distress. It addresses defects, safety, obsolescence, asset impairments, purchase commitments, and intellectual-property licensing or infringement. Other risks include dependence on developers, digital-content providers, employees, carriers and resellers; App Store changes; reseller investments; IT outages, cyberattacks and data breaches; and investments, acquisitions and retail operations, including returns, costs, leases and closures.

title: Legal and Regulatory Compliance Risks
key_items: The Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition could be adversely impacted by unfavorable results of legal proceedings or government investigations.
The Company is subject to complex and changing laws and regulations worldwide, which exposes the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.

The technology industry, including, in some instances, the Company, is subject to intense media, political and regulatory scrutiny, which exposes the Company to increasing regulation, government investigations, legal actions and penalties.
The Company’s business is subject to a variety of U.S. and international laws, rules, policies and other obligations regarding data protection.
summary: The Company faces growing legal claims, investigations and indemnity exposure, especially patent litigation, which can be costly and disruptive; settlements may raise expenses or restrict products and practices. Outcomes could bring substantial damages, injunctions or other remedies and materially harm results, despite limited insurance. Complex, changing global regulations across competition, privacy, trade, tax, labor, environmental and other areas increase compliance costs and risks. Technology-industry scrutiny, antitrust matters, App Store litigation and proposed laws may force business changes, fines and harm users, partners, reputation, demand and sales. Data-protection laws impose costly, evolving duties for personal and sensitive information; violations or inconsistent privacy statements can trigger audits, penalties and liability. Health-data breaches and payment-card noncompliance can bring investigations, fines, higher transaction costs or loss of payment processing.

title: Financial Risks
key_items: The Company expects its quarterly net sales and results of operations to fluctuate.
The Company’s financial performance is subject to risks associated with changes in the value of the U.S. dollar relative to local currencies.
The Company is exposed to credit risk and fluctuations in the values of its investment portfolio.

The Company is exposed to credit risk on its trade accounts receivable, vendor non-trade receivables and prepayments related to long-term supply agreements, and this risk is heightened during periods when economic conditions worsen.
The Company is subject to changes in tax rates, the adoption of new U.S. or international tax legislation and exposure to additional tax liabilities.
summary: The Company’s quarterly sales, margins and results may fluctuate due to seasonality, product concentration and demand, launches, pricing and competition, costs, product mix, operational disruptions, and other factors. Currency movements can affect foreign sales, costs and margins; pricing responses and hedging may not offset these effects. Investments face market, liquidity and credit risks, while unsecured customer and vendor receivables and supply-chain prepayments may cause losses, particularly in downturns. Changes in tax laws, rates, earnings mix, or tax audit outcomes could increase tax liabilities and materially harm results and financial condition.

title: Stock Risks, Properties, and Legal Matters
key_items: The price of the Company’s stock is subject to volatility.
Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments; Item 2. Properties; Item 4. Mine Safety Disclosures
summary: Discusses stock-price volatility and the risk that unmet expectations for growth, dividends, or buybacks could harm investor confidence and employee retention. Reports no unresolved staff comments, describes the company’s facilities and their condition, and notes ordinary-course legal proceedings and their potential financial impact. Details the Epic Games App Store antitrust case, the 2021 ruling, injunction, and appeals. Mine safety disclosures are not applicable.

title: Stock Listing, Holders, and Repurchases
key_items: Item 5. Market for Registrant’s Common Equity, Related Stockholder Matters and Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities
Purchases of Equity Securities by the Issuer and Affiliated Purchasers
summary: Part II, Item 5 reports that Apple common stock trades on Nasdaq under AAPL and had 23,502 shareholders of record as of October 15, 2021. It details share repurchases during the quarter ended September 25, 2021, including monthly share counts and average prices, and explains the $315 billion repurchase authorization, $254.1 billion used, and $60.9 billion remaining. It also describes completion of the May 2021 $5 billion accelerated repurchase agreement: 36 million shares delivered at an average $137.20.

title: Stock Performance and Reserved Item 6
summary: Compares Apple’s dividend-reinvested cumulative shareholder returns over the five years ended September 25, 2021, with the S&P 500, S&P Information Technology, and Dow Jones U.S. Technology Supersector indexes, assuming $100 invested in each on September 23, 2016. It provides annual performance figures, data-point timing, and index copyright notices, and cautions that past performance does not predict future results. Item 6 is reserved.

title: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
summary: The MD&A should be read alongside the consolidated financial statements and notes in Part II, Item 8. It generally covers fiscal 2021 and 2020 and compares those years; discussion of 2019 and comparisons of 2020 with 2019 are available in the company’s 2020 Form 10-K, Part II, Item 7.

title: Fiscal Year Highlights
key_items: iPhone; Mac; iPad; Wearables, Home and Accessories; Services
summary: The text outlines COVID-19’s global and company-specific effects, including closures, remote work, reopening under safety restrictions, supplier and logistics disruptions that constrained sales, and uncertainty about future impacts. In 2021, sales rose 33% ($91.3 billion) across all categories and segments; Apple expanded its repurchase authorization and dividend, repurchased $85.5 billion in stock, and paid $14.5 billion in dividends. It reports category sales for 2019–2021 and explains growth drivers: new iPhone models and sales mix; MacBook and iMac; iPad Air and Pro; accessories and Apple Watch; and advertising, App Store, and cloud services. Notes clarify category accounting and included products and services.

title: Segment Operating Performance
key_items: Products Gross Margin; Services Gross Margin
summary: The Company reports results across five geographic segments: Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific, with regional definitions and management rationale provided. The text presents 2019–2021 segment sales and explains 2021 increases, mainly from iPhone, Services, iPad, or Mac sales, with favorable currency effects in Europe, Greater China, and Rest of Asia Pacific. It reports product and Services gross margins and percentages; 2021 increases reflected sales volume, mix, leverage, and currency, partly offset by higher Services costs. Future margins may be volatile and face downward pressure. Operating expense figures and growth are shown; R&D growth reflected staffing, professional services, and infrastructure, while SG&A growth reflected staffing, variable selling, and professional services. The Company emphasizes R&D’s importance to growth, competitiveness, and product and service development.

title: Operating Expenses
summary: The text reports Apple’s 2019–2021 gross margins and percentages, explaining 2021 product and services increases and warning margins may remain volatile and face downward pressure. It gives operating-expense figures and attributes 2021 R&D and SG&A growth to staffing, services, infrastructure, and selling costs, while emphasizing R&D investment. It summarizes lower 2021 other income/expense, tax rates and their drivers, and a $3.5 billion valuation-allowance increase with no net-income effect. Liquidity was $172.6 billion, expected to meet needs and capital returns; debt obligations included $118.1 billion in notes, related interest, and $6.0 billion of commercial paper.

title: Provision for Income Taxes
summary: The text reports 2021, 2020, and 2019 other income and expense and income-tax figures. Net other income/expense fell in 2021, primarily because of lower interest income and marketable-securities losses, partly offset by favorable non-marketable-security fair-value adjustments and lower term-debt interest expense. Effective tax rates were below the 21% federal statutory rate in all three years; reasons included lower rates on foreign earnings and share-based compensation benefits, with 2021 also benefiting from foreign-derived intangible income deductions and changes in unrecognized tax benefits. The year-over-year tax-rate decline was partly offset by a one-time 2020 foreign-tax-credit adjustment. In 2021, Ireland foreign-tax-credit and California R&D-credit carryforwards increased the valuation allowance by $3.5 billion without affecting net income; management expects to realize substantially all remaining deferred tax assets.

title: Liquidity and Capital Resources
key_items: Leases; Manufacturing Purchase Obligations; Other Purchase Obligations; Deemed Repatriation Tax Payable
summary: Apple reported $172.6 billion in cash, cash equivalents and unrestricted marketable securities and expects these resources, operating cash flow and debt-market access to cover cash needs and capital returns. At September 25, 2021, obligations included $118.1 billion in notes ($9.6 billion due within a year) and $39.5 billion in related interest ($2.9 billion due), $6.0 billion in commercial paper, $14.6 billion in leases ($1.8 billion due), $54.8 billion in primarily noncancelable manufacturing purchases ($54.7 billion due), $8.3 billion in other purchases ($4.8 billion due), and $24.6 billion in repatriation tax, none due within a year. The Board-authorized share repurchase program has no fixed purchase commitment; the quarterly dividend was $0.22 per share, with annual increases intended subject to Board approval.

title: Critical Accounting Estimates
summary: Management’s financial estimates rely on GAAP policies, historical experience, and reasonable assumptions. Uncertain tax positions across U.S. and foreign jurisdictions and ordinary-course legal claims require judgment; differing outcomes could materially affect results. Apple reviews currency and interest-rate hedges, which may not fully offset exposures or align in accounting timing. Interest-rate risks involve investments and debt: a 100-basis-point rise could reduce portfolio fair value by $4.1 billion (2021) or $3.1 billion (2020), and raise annualized debt interest by $186 million or $218 million. Apple manages currency risk with forwards and options, typically hedging forecast revenue and inventory exposures for up to 12 months; dollar strength can hurt sales and margins.

title: Market Risk and Interest Rate Management
key_items: Interest Rate and Foreign Currency Risk Management
summary: The Company reviews foreign-exchange forwards and options and interest-rate swaps, but they may only partly offset exposure, and hedge gains or losses may be recognized at different times from underlying effects. Interest-rate exposure primarily involves investments and debt, with U.S. rates most influential. Its capital-preservation investment strategy uses mainly investment-grade securities with issuer limits. A 100-basis-point rate increase would reduce portfolio fair value by $4.1 billion in 2021 and $3.1 billion in 2020, with losses realized only if sold before maturity. Debt totaled $118.7 billion and $107.4 billion, respectively; swaps manage rate exposure, and a 100-basis-point increase would raise annualized interest expense by $186 million and $218 million.

title: Foreign Currency Risk
summary: The Company is a net receiver of foreign currencies, so a stronger U.S. dollar can reduce reported sales and gross margins and may force local price changes amid currency volatility. It uses forwards and options to hedge selected assets, liabilities, commitments, forecast cash flows, subsidiary investments, and debt-related currency effects, typically hedging forecast revenue and inventory exposure for up to 12 months, but may leave exposures unhedged for accounting or cost reasons. A Monte Carlo VAR analysis of derivatives, excluding underlying exposures, estimated a 95%-confidence maximum one-day fair-value loss of $550 million in 2021 versus $551 million in 2020; hedge gains and losses generally offset. Actual outcomes may differ materially because of prediction and exposure limitations.

title: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
summary: Item 8 indexes Apple’s consolidated financial statements: statements of operations, comprehensive income, shareholders’ equity, and cash flows for fiscal 2021, 2020, and 2019; balance sheets for 2021 and 2020; notes; and independent auditor reports, with page references. Financial statement schedules are omitted because they are inapplicable, immaterial in amount, or included in the statements and notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF OPERATIONS
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated statements of operations present results for the years ended September 28, 2019, September 26, 2020, and September 25, 2021, in millions except shares (in thousands) and per-share amounts. They report product and services net sales, corresponding costs and gross margin; research and development and selling, general and administrative expenses; operating income, other income or expense, pretax income, income tax provision, net income, basic and diluted earnings per share, and basic and diluted weighted-average shares. The statements refer readers to the accompanying notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME
summary: Apple’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income report net income, other comprehensive income or loss, and total comprehensive income for fiscal years ended September 25, 2021, September 26, 2020, and September 28, 2019. Other comprehensive items include foreign currency translation, derivative gains and losses (fair-value changes and amounts realized in net income), and marketable debt security gains and losses (fair-value changes and amounts realized in net income), all net of tax. The statements are in millions and refer readers to the accompanying financial statement notes.

title: Apple Inc. Consolidated Balance Sheets
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated balance sheets present assets, liabilities, commitments and contingencies, and shareholders’ equity as of September 25, 2021 and September 26, 2020. They detail current and non-current asset and liability categories, share-capital information, retained earnings, and accumulated other comprehensive income or loss, with totals for assets, liabilities, and equity. Amounts are in millions except shares, stated in thousands, and par value.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF SHAREHOLDERS’ EQUITY
summary: Apple’s consolidated statements of shareholders’ equity report beginning and ending equity balances for the years ended September 28, 2019, September 26, 2020, and September 25, 2021. They detail changes in common stock and paid-in capital, retained earnings, and accumulated other comprehensive income or loss, including stock issuance, compensation, net income, dividends, share withholding, repurchases, and accounting-principle changes. Ending equity was $90.488 billion, $65.339 billion, and $63.090 billion, respectively; declared dividends per share or RSU were $0.75, $0.795, and $0.85. Amounts are in millions except per-share figures; accompanying notes apply.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS (intro)
nodes.summary: Apple’s 2021 Form 10-K excerpt presents consolidated cash flows for fiscal 2021, 2020 and 2019, covering operating, investing and financing activities, changes in cash, ending balances and supplemental cash taxes and interest paid. It also summarizes accounting policies: consolidated entities and eliminations, estimates, reclassifications and fiscal-year timing; adoption of the credit-loss standard without material impact; advertising expense recognition; share-based compensation measurement; and basic and diluted EPS calculations, including net income, weighted-average shares and per-share results.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies and Recent Pronouncement
nodes.summary: Apple’s consolidated statements include its wholly owned subsidiaries, eliminate intercompany items, and include normal recurring adjustments. Preparation under U.S. GAAP requires estimates that may differ from actual results; prior-period amounts were reclassified. Its fiscal year ends on the last Saturday of September, spans 52 or 53 weeks, and included 52 weeks in 2019–2021. Apple adopted the expected-credit-loss standard in 2021 using modified retrospective transition, with no material impact. Advertising is expensed as incurred in selling, general and administrative expenses. Share-based compensation is generally valued at the stock’s closing price on grant date and expensed straight-line over estimated vesting.

nodes.title: Earnings Per Share
nodes.summary: Reports Apple’s basic and diluted EPS for 2021–2019, treasury-stock-method accounting, and antidilutive securities excluded in 2019. Describes policies for cash equivalents and marketable debt and equity securities, including classification, fair-value effects, and sale-cost identification; FIFO inventory; straight-line depreciation and software amortization, related expenses, and 2019 noncash property transactions; and classification of restricted cash and securities. Explains derivative fair-value accounting and treatment of cash-flow hedges, fair-value hedges, excluded hedge components, and non-designated derivatives.

nodes.title: Financial Asset and Property Accounting Policies
key_items: Restricted Cash and Restricted Marketable Securities
nodes.summary: The Company uses the treasury stock method for diluted EPS and excluded 62 million potentially dilutive shares in 2019 as antidilutive. Cash equivalents have purchase-date maturities of three months or less. Available-for-sale debt securities are classified by contractual maturity, with unrealized gains and losses in OCI; equity securities are measured at fair value with gains and losses in OI&E. Securities sold use specific identification, and inventories use FIFO. Property and equipment and internal-use software are depreciated or amortized straight-line over specified useful lives; related expense was $9.5 billion, $9.7 billion, and $11.3 billion in 2021, 2020, and 2019. 2019 noncash property transactions reduced payables and other current liabilities by $2.9 billion. Legally restricted cash and securities are classified and reported according to restriction duration and underlying security classification.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments and Hedging
nodes.summary: Derivative instruments are recorded at fair value, with gains and losses accounted for according to hedge designation: cash flow hedge amounts are deferred in AOCI and later recognized with the hedged item; fair value hedge amounts and offsets enter earnings. Excluded option time value and forward carry are recognized over the hedge term, while related fair-value changes go to OCI. Non-hedge changes enter earnings; derivatives are presented gross and cash flows classified as operating. Fair-value methods use quoted prices or observable-data-based models. Revenue policies cover transfer of control, returns and incentives, allocation among distinct obligations using stand-alone selling prices, recognition of hardware and deferred bundled services/software, undelivered long-term services, gross versus net third-party sales, and exclusion of customer taxes remitted to authorities.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements and Revenue Recognition
nodes.summary: The page explains derivative presentation and cash flow classification, and fair-value methods for marketable securities, debt, and other financial instruments. It describes revenue recognition for products and services, returns and incentives, allocation of transaction prices among distinct obligations using stand-alone selling prices, timing of recognition and related costs, treatment of undelivered long-term services, gross versus net reporting for third-party sales, and exclusion of customer taxes from revenue.

nodes.title: Deferred Revenue
nodes.summary: Deferred revenue was $11.9 billion as of September 25, 2021, compared with $10.2 billion as of September 26, 2020. The Company expects the 2021 balance to be realized 64% within one year, 26% in one to two years, 8% in two to three years, and 2% after more than three years.

nodes.title: Disaggregated Revenue
nodes.summary: Apple reports 2021–2019 net sales by product and service category, explains what each category includes, notes revenue recognized from prior-year deferred revenue, and says sales mix was generally consistent across reportable segments. It details 2021 and 2020 cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities by investment type, fair value hierarchy, cost, gains/losses, and balance-sheet classification; identifies restricted securities; and explains fair-value methods. It also gives 2021 non-current debt-security maturities and describes its investment-grade, issuer-limited policy focused on minimizing principal-loss risk and possible reasons for early sales.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments and Hedging
nodes.summary: The text describes the Company’s use of derivatives to partly manage foreign-exchange and interest-rate risks, including hedging strategies, instruments, durations, notional amounts, hedged-item balances, and the immateriality of related fair values and recognized gains or losses. It outlines trade-receivable credit protections and customer concentration, plus vendor non-trade receivable concentrations for 2021 and 2020. It also presents comparative consolidated balances for property, plant and equipment and other non-current liabilities.

nodes.title: Receivables, Fair Value Hedges and Property Details
key_items: Note 4 – Consolidated Financial Statement Details; Property, Plant and Equipment, Net
nodes.summary: Reports fair-value-hedged marketable securities and term debt carrying amounts for 2021 and 2020, noting related gains and losses were immaterial in 2019–2021. Describes trade-receivable credit-risk protections and customer concentration, and vendor non-trade receivables from component sales and vendor concentrations. Presents 2021 and 2020 property, plant and equipment categories, gross totals, accumulated depreciation and amortization, and net totals.

nodes.title: Other Non-Current Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s other non-current liabilities for 2021 and 2020: long-term taxes payable, other non-current liabilities, and their totals. It also details other income/(expense), net for 2021, 2020, and 2019, breaking it down into interest and dividend income, interest expense, other income/(expense), and the total.

nodes.title: Note 5 – Income Taxes Provision for Income Taxes and Effective Tax Rate
nodes.summary: The note reports income tax provisions by federal, state, and foreign current and deferred taxes for 2021–2019, foreign pretax earnings, and reconciles statutory 21% expected tax to actual provision and effective rates (13.3%, 14.4%, and 15.9%). It presents 2021 and 2020 deferred tax asset and liability components and net balances, explains their measurement and the elected treatment of certain Act-related minimum-tax items, and discloses indefinite Irish foreign tax-credit and California R&D-credit carryforwards and a valuation allowance.

nodes.title: Uncertain Tax Positions
nodes.summary: As of September 25, 2021, gross unrecognized tax benefits were $15.5 billion, including $6.6 billion that would affect the effective tax rate; the comparable 2020 amounts were $16.5 billion and $8.8 billion. The text details 2019–2021 changes in these balances, excluding interest and penalties, from prior- and current-year tax positions, settlements, and statute expirations. Apple files in U.S. federal, state, and foreign jurisdictions; certain years remain open to examination, and benefits may decrease by up to $1.2 billion within 12 months.

nodes.title: Tax Interest, Penalties, and European State Aid
nodes.summary: The Company records income-tax-related interest and penalties in its tax provision; accrued totals were $1.5 billion in 2021 and $1.4 billion in 2020, with annual expenses of $219 million, $85 million, and $73 million in 2021, 2020, and 2019. The European Commission’s 2016 decision ordered Ireland to recover taxes for 2003–2014 based on tax opinions, totaling €13.1 billion plus interest. The General Court annulled the decision in 2020, and the Commission appealed. The Company believes any incremental Irish taxes could be creditable against U.S. taxes, subject to limitations. Annual requests may reduce recovery for taxes paid elsewhere; the adjusted amount was €12.7 billion as of September 2021. Recovery plus interest is held in restricted escrow pending legal proceedings.

nodes.title: Note 6 – Leases
nodes.summary: Note 6 describes leases for equipment and retail, corporate, manufacturing, and data-center facilities, typically with terms up to 10 years and renewal options; certain lease and nonlease components are combined. It reports fixed and variable lease costs, prior-year rent expense, cash payments, and noncash right-of-use asset activity for 2019–2021. It presents 2020–2021 right-of-use assets and lease liabilities by type and financial-statement line, 2021 liability maturities, remaining lease terms and discount rates, and $1.1 billion of future payments for leases not yet commenced. Note 7, Debt, begins.

nodes.title: Commercial Paper and Repurchase Agreements
nodes.summary: The Company’s commercial paper program provides unsecured short-term funding for general corporate purposes, including dividends and share repurchases. Outstanding balances were $6.0 billion in 2021 and $5.0 billion in 2020, generally maturing within nine months, with weighted-average rates of 0.06% and 0.62%, respectively. A table reports issuance and repayment cash flows for 2019–2021, including maturities of 90 days or less and longer maturities. In 2020, the Company entered into $5.2 billion of repurchase agreements, accounted for as collateralized borrowings due to its continuing involvement; all were settled by year-end.

nodes.title: Term Debt
nodes.summary: Apple’s term debt totaled $118.1 billion in 2021, compared with $106.1 billion in 2020, with varied maturities, rates, hedging adjustments, current/non-current portions, future principal payments and Level 2 fair values. Interest-rate and foreign-currency swaps manage risk; term-debt interest expense was $2.6 billion in 2021, $2.8 billion in 2020 and $3.2 billion in 2019. The company’s $315 billion repurchase authorization had $254.1 billion used by 2021 after repurchasing 656 million shares for $85.5 billion; annual share movements for 2019–2021 are reported. The text describes employee and director equity plans, vesting, dividend rights, reserved shares and plan expiry, and identifies five officers with Rule 10b5-1 trading plans.

nodes.title: Apple Equity, Benefit Plans and Trading
key_items: Apple Inc. Non-Employee Director Stock Plan
nodes.summary: The page reports Apple’s share repurchase authorization, 2021 repurchases and cumulative program use, and changes in common shares outstanding from 2019–2021. It describes the employee and non-employee director stock plans, including eligible awards, vesting and dividend rights, share-count rules, future share reserves, and the Director Plan’s expiration. It also identifies officers with Rule 10b5-1 trading plans and explains how those plans preestablish stock-trading terms.

nodes.title: Employee Plans and Share-Based Compensation
nodes.summary: Describes the employee stock purchase plan’s eligibility, discounted purchase price, payroll and annual limits, and shares reserved; the 401(k) plan’s employee deferrals and service-based company match; RSU grants, vesting, cancellations, balances, fair values, tax-related share withholding, and tax payments for 2019–2021; annual share-based compensation expense and tax benefits; and unrecognized RSU and stock-option compensation costs and expected recognition period.

nodes.title: Share-Based Compensation
nodes.summary: The text describes Apple’s employee benefits: an employee stock purchase plan with discounted shares, contribution and annual purchase limits, and shares reserved; a 401(k) plan with employee deferrals and service-based company matching; and RSU activity, vesting values, tax-related share withholding, and payments. It reports share-based compensation expense, tax benefits, and unrecognized costs. It also covers warranty accruals and the iPhone Upgrade Program’s guarantee accounting; risks from component sourcing, shortages, pricing, custom parts, supplier agreements, and outsourced manufacturing; and future payments under unconditional purchase obligations.

nodes.title: Commitments, Supply Risks, and Purchase Obligations
key_items: Concentrations in the Available Sources of Supply of Materials and Product
nodes.summary: The page reports warranty accrual activity for 2019–2021 and explains the iPhone Upgrade Program’s trade-in guarantee accounting. It describes risks from limited-source and custom components, industry shortages and price fluctuations, supplier capacity and contract uncertainty, and reliance on outsourced manufacturing, primarily in Asia. It also outlines off-balance-sheet unconditional purchase obligations for content, internet and telecommunications services, and supplier arrangements, with future noncancelable payments totaling $8.184 billion.

nodes.title: Contingencies
key_items: VirnetX; iOS Performance Management Cases; French Competition Authority; Optis
nodes.summary: The Company faces ordinary-course legal claims, accruing probable and estimable losses; management sees no material loss reasonably possible beyond the matters described, though unfavorable outcomes exceeding expectations could materially affect results. VirnetX won a $503 million patent verdict in a 2020 retrial, which the Company appealed; the PTO invalidated the patents, subject to VirnetX’s appeal. U.S. iOS performance-management class actions settled for $310 million, with final approval in 2021; the Company maintains its feature was beneficial and disclosures proper. France’s competition authority fined the Company €1.1 billion, which it disputes and appeals. Optis received a $300 million patent-damages award after retrial; the Company plans to appeal.

nodes.title: Note 11 – Segment Information and Geographic Data
nodes.summary: The note explains Apple’s management-based segment reporting across five geographic regions, defines their boundaries, and states that policies follow Note 1. Segments are assessed by net sales and operating income; it describes how these are attributed and which corporate costs, other items, and intersegment transfers are excluded. It presents 2019–2021 regional sales and operating income, reconciliations to consolidated operating income, geographic sales and long-lived assets, and notes that only the U.S. and China exceeded 10% of sales, no customer exceeded 10%, and China includes Hong Kong and Taiwan.

summary: Presents Apple’s 2019–2021 consolidated cash flows and accounting policies, including EPS, investments, property, derivatives, hedging, revenue, deferred and disaggregated sales, fair values, receivables, and liabilities. Covers income taxes, uncertain tax positions and European state aid; leases, commercial paper, repurchase agreements and term debt; share repurchases, equity and employee benefit plans, share-based compensation, warranties, supply risks, purchase commitments and legal contingencies. Reports geographic segments, sales, operating income and long-lived assets.

title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm

nodes.title: Apple Independent Auditor’s Report
nodes.summary: The auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Apple’s 2021 and 2020 balance sheets and three years of related financial statements conform to U.S. GAAP, and reports an unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting as of September 25, 2021. The report explains management’s responsibility, auditor independence and PCAOB audit standards, procedures, and reasonable-assurance basis. It defines the critical audit matter and clarifies it does not change or create a separate opinion; the page ends at its description heading.

nodes.title: Uncertain Tax Positions
nodes.summary: The text describes Apple’s uncertain tax positions: $15.5 billion in gross unrecognized tax benefits at September 25, 2021, including $6.6 billion that would affect its effective tax rate, and the judgment involved in assessing them. EY outlines audit procedures, including control testing, review of management analyses and tax-authority communications, tax specialists’ assessments, legal confirmations and advisor discussions, and disclosure review. EY then reports that Apple maintained effective internal control over financial reporting under COSO criteria, explains the audit basis and procedures, defines these controls and their purposes, and notes their inherent limitations and risks over time. EY also notes its unqualified financial-statement opinion and service as auditor since 2009.

nodes.title: Apple Internal Control Audit Report
key_items: Opinion on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
Definition and Limitations of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Ernst & Young opines that Apple maintained effective internal control over financial reporting as of September 25, 2021, under COSO criteria, and notes its separate unqualified opinion on Apple’s financial statements. The report outlines management’s and auditors’ responsibilities, PCAOB audit standards and procedures, and the basis for the opinion. It defines financial reporting controls and their purposes, while noting limits on preventing or detecting misstatements and risks in applying evaluations to future periods.

nodes.title: Accountant Changes and Internal Controls
key_items: Item 9. Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants on Accounting and Financial Disclosure
Evaluation of Disclosure Controls and Procedures
Management’s Annual Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: The Company reports no changes or disagreements with accountants. Management concluded disclosure controls were effective as of September 25, 2021. The page describes internal controls’ purposes and inherent limits: they offer reasonable, not absolute, assurance, may not prevent or detect all errors or fraud, and can weaken as conditions or compliance change. Management assessed financial-reporting controls using the 2013 COSO framework and found them effective as of that date; Ernst & Young issued an audit report included in Part II, Item 8.

nodes.title: Changes in Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Apple reported no fourth-quarter 2021 changes to internal control over financial reporting that materially affected or were likely to materially affect it. Under Exchange Act Section 13(r), Apple disclosed that after the FSB was designated a blocked party in March 2021, an OFAC general license permitted certain regulatory dealings; Apple filed required Russian import notifications, made no payments or earned revenue or profit, and may engage further in compliance with U.S. law. Foreign-jurisdiction inspection disclosure was not applicable. Items on directors, compensation, ownership, related transactions and independence, and auditor fees and services are incorporated from the forthcoming 2022 Proxy Statement.

nodes.title: Regulatory Disclosures and Part III Proxy Matters
key_items: Disclosure Pursuant to Section 13(r) of the Exchange Act; Item 9C. Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictions that Prevent Inspections
Disclosure Pursuant to Section 13(r) of the Exchange Act
Item 9C. Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictions that Prevent Inspections
Item 10. Directors, Executive Officers and Corporate Governance
Item 12. Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners and Management and Related Stockholder Matters
Item 13. Certain Relationships and Related Transactions, and Director Independence
Item 14. Principal Accountant Fees and Services
nodes.summary: Reports Apple’s Section 13(r) disclosure concerning legally required FSB notifications for Russian product imports under an authorized general license; no payments, revenue, or profits resulted, and future compliant engagement is possible. Item 9C is not applicable. Part III items on directors, executive compensation, ownership, related transactions and director independence, and accountant fees and services refer to the 2022 Proxy Statement, to be filed within 120 days after September 25, 2021.

summary: Reports EY’s unqualified opinions that Apple’s 2021 and 2020 financial statements comply with U.S. GAAP and that internal controls were effective as of September 25, 2021. Describes management and auditor responsibilities, audit standards, procedures, reasonable assurance, control purposes and limitations, and the critical audit matter concerning uncertain tax positions ($15.5 billion in gross unrecognized benefits). Reports no accountant disagreements or material fourth-quarter control changes. Discloses authorized FSB-related Russian import notifications with no payments or revenue, notes foreign-inspection disclosure is inapplicable, and refers Part III proxy matters to Apple’s 2022 Proxy Statement.

title: PART IV
summary: Part IV of Apple’s 2021 Form 10-K lists the filed financial statements and their page references; explains that financial statement schedules are omitted as inapplicable, immaterial, or included elsewhere; and catalogs exhibits incorporated by reference or filed/furnished, including corporate documents, debt indentures and note certificates, compensation and equity plans, subsidiaries, auditor consent, power of attorney, executive certifications, and Inline XBRL files. It identifies management-compensation exhibits and notes that omitted long-term debt instruments will be supplied to the SEC upon request. Item 16 states there is no Form 10-K summary.

title: SIGNATURES
summary: Apple’s October 28, 2021 Form 10-K signature page states that Luca Maestri signed the report for the company under the Securities Exchange Act. It grants Timothy D. Cook and Luca Maestri joint and several power of attorney to sign and file amendments and related materials. The report lists signatures, titles, and the same date for ten officers and directors: Cook, Maestri, Chris Kondo, James A. Bell, Al Gore, Andrea Jung, Arthur D. Levinson, Monica Lozano, Ronald D. Sugar, and Susan L. Wagner.

title: DESCRIPTION OF THE REGISTRANT’S SECURITIES REGISTERED PURSUANT TO SECTION 12 OF THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934
summary: As of September 25, 2021, Apple had 11 securities registered under Section 12 of the Exchange Act: common stock and 10 note issues with stated interest rates and maturities from 2022 through 2042. All were listed on The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC.

title: DESCRIPTION OF COMMON STOCK
key_items: Dividends; Right to Receive Liquidation Distributions; No Preemptive or Similar Rights
Anti-Takeover Provisions of the Articles, Bylaws and California Law; Listing
Anti-Takeover Provisions of the Articles, Bylaws and California Law
summary: The text outlines Apple common stock rights under its Articles, Bylaws and California law: 50.4 billion shares are authorized, and outstanding shares are fully paid and nonassessable. Each share has one vote, without cumulative voting; it describes approval thresholds, director elections and removal, vacancy filling, amendments, and meeting adjournments. Holders may receive board-declared lawful dividends and pro rata liquidation distributions, but have no preemptive, conversion, redemption or sinking-fund rights. Anti-takeover provisions cover board vacancies, advance notice, proxy-access nominations, special meetings and California’s fairness-opinion requirement for interested-party reorganizations. The stock trades on Nasdaq as AAPL.

title: DESCRIPTION OF DEBT SECURITIES

nodes.title: The Notes
key_items: The 2022 Notes; The 2024 Notes; The 0.000% 2025 Notes; The 0.875% 2025 Notes; The 2026 Notes
The 2027 Notes; The 1.375% 2029 Notes; The 3.050% 2029 Notes; The 2031 Notes; The 2042 Notes
nodes.summary: The text summarizes Apple’s euro- and sterling-denominated Notes, subject to two indentures with BNY Mellon dated 2013 and 2018 and governed by New York law. The indentures permit unlimited debt issuance and, without existing holders’ consent, additional similar securities that may join a series, subject to ISIN conditions. It lists ten outstanding note issues—the 2022, 2024, two 2025, 2026, 2027, two 2029, 2031 and 2042 Notes—giving each issue’s principal amount, issuance and maturity dates, annual or semiannual interest rate and payment schedule, and amount outstanding as of October 15, 2021.

nodes.title: Ranking
nodes.summary: The Notes rank equally with the issuer’s other senior unsecured, unsubordinated debt, but are structurally subordinated to subsidiary debt and preferred stock and effectively subordinated to secured debt up to the value of its collateral. Subsidiary creditors, including trade creditors and preferred stockholders, generally have priority over Noteholders in subsidiary assets and earnings. The Indentures do not limit the issuer or its subsidiaries from incurring additional debt.

nodes.title: Payment on the Notes
nodes.summary: Payments on the 2022, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027, 2029 (1.375%) and 2031 Notes are payable in euros, but switch to U.S. dollars if euros become unavailable or cease to be used for specified monetary purposes. Conversion uses the Federal Reserve rate or, if none is set, the latest Wall Street Journal rate available two Business Days before payment; dollar payment is not a default. Their Business Day definition requires New York and London banks to be open and TARGET2 operating. The 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes are payable in pounds sterling, or euros if the UK adopts the euro, with comparable dollar-payment, conversion and no-default provisions. Their Business Day definition excludes closures in New York, London or the payment location.

nodes.title: Payment of Additional Amounts
nodes.summary: The Notes generally require principal and interest payments free of U.S. tax withholding unless legally required. The Company must pay non-U.S. holders additional amounts to preserve the stated net payment, subject to exceptions for holder-specific U.S. connections or tax status; intermediary ownership or fiduciary arrangements; failures to provide required tax certifications; non-withholding taxes; late-effective legal changes; specified transfer, estate, sales and similar taxes; availability of another paying agent; late presentation; FATCA-related taxes; and combinations of these exclusions. The Notes remain subject to applicable tax laws, and no other tax payments are required. The text defines the United States and United States person for these provisions and tax-related redemption provisions.

nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons
nodes.summary: If U.S. tax-law changes or changes in official interpretations announced or effective on or after the relevant prospectus supplement require, or independent counsel concludes will require, additional payments for a note series, the issuer may redeem that series in full, but not partially, at 100% of principal plus accrued unpaid interest (excluding the redemption date for the 0.000% 2025 and 2031 Notes). Prior notice is 30–60 days for the 2022, 2024, 2026, 2027, 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes; 15–60 days for the 0.875% 2025 and 1.375% 2029 Notes; and 10–60 days for the 0.000% 2025 and 2031 Notes.

nodes.title: Optional Redemption
nodes.summary: The text sets optional redemption terms for specified notes. The 2022, 2024, 2026, 2027, 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes may be redeemed at any time at the greater of par or a discounted-value price based on remaining payments and specified yield spreads. The 0.000% and 0.875% 2025, 1.375% 2029 and 2031 Notes have similar make-whole redemption pricing before their defined Par Call Dates; afterward, they may be redeemed at par. It specifies Par Call Dates, payment of accrued interest and scheduled interest, and definitions of the applicable German or UK Comparable Government Bond and the Comparable Government Bond Rate, determined using market yields three business days before redemption.

nodes.title: Covenants
key_items: Consolidation, Merger and Sale of Assets
nodes.summary: The Indentures contain limited covenants and do not restrict the amount of debt or leases, debt secured by liens, or dividends, distributions, and purchases or redemptions of capital stock. They permit mergers, consolidations, or transfers of substantially all assets if the successor is appropriately organized in the U.S., assumes the obligations and any conversion rights, no default exists after the transaction, and, under the 2013 Indenture, the trustee receives an officers’ certificate and counsel’s opinion. The successor replaces the issuer and assumes its rights and obligations, releasing the issuer. “Person” includes individuals, entities, governments, and their agencies or subdivisions.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: The indentures define series-specific defaults: 30-day interest nonpayment; principal or premium nonpayment when due; uncured covenant breaches after 90 days’ notice (holder thresholds are 25% under the 2013 Indenture and 33% under the 2018); specified voluntary or court-ordered bankruptcy, insolvency, or liquidation events; and other series-specific defaults. Bankruptcy terms are defined, and court orders must generally remain effective for 90 days. For continuing non-bankruptcy defaults, the trustee or threshold holders may accelerate debt; bankruptcy defaults trigger automatic acceleration. A majority may rescind acceleration if required sums are deposited and other defaults cured or waived. Defaults are series-specific. The issuer must provide the trustee an annual officer’s compliance statement. Individual holders may pursue proceedings only after specified notice, holder-request, indemnity, trustee-delay, and no-majority-direction conditions. A majority may direct remedies and waive certain defaults; the trustee’s duties and indemnity protections are described. Each holder retains an unconditional right to payment when due and to sue for it.

nodes.title: Modification and Waivers
nodes.summary: Indenture and Note amendments generally require consent from holders of a majority of the affected series, but changes to key payment, redemption, currency, enforcement, voting, waiver, or conversion rights require each affected holder’s consent. The issuer and trustee may make specified changes without consent, including adding protections, defaults, guarantees, security, trustees or securities; adapting series terms and formats; curing defects; making non-material changes; and complying with legal, exchange, or depository rules. A series majority may waive certain covenants and past defaults, except payment defaults and provisions requiring individual consent; waivers cure only the specific default and do not affect later defaults.

nodes.title: Discharge, Defeasance and Covenant Defeasance
nodes.summary: The text explains discharge by depositing sufficient U.S. dollars for Notes due or redeemable within a year, and legal or covenant defeasance through an irrevocable, sufficient deposit of cash and/or qualifying government obligations. Legal defeasance preserves certain administrative and payment-in-trust duties; covenant defeasance releases restrictive-covenant duties, though funds may not cover accelerated payments and the issuer remains liable. It defines German government obligations for specified euro Notes and UK government obligations for the 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes, states tax-opinion requirements, and permits legal defeasance after covenant defeasance. Notes are book-entry global securities held through Euroclear and Clearstream; definitive certificates may be issued under specified depositary, issuer-election, or default conditions, with currency-specific denominations. The Bank of New York Mellon Trust Company, N.A. serves as trustee and has existing and potential future banking, custody, trustee, and paying-agent relationships with the issuer.

nodes.title: Note Defeasance, Settlement, Certificates, and Trustee
nodes.summary: Defines eligible U.K. government obligations for certain notes and requires a tax opinion for defeasance; legal defeasance may follow covenant defeasance. Notes are issued as global book-entry securities through Euroclear and Clearstream. Under specified conditions, global notes may be exchanged for certificated notes in stated euro or sterling denominations, including if the depositary cannot continue, the issuer opts out of global form, or a continuing default occurs. The Bank of New York Mellon Trust Company, N.A. is trustee and has existing and potential future banking, custodial, trustee, and paying-agent relationships with the issuer.

Also lists Exhibit 21.1.

title: Consent of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
summary: Ernst & Young consents to incorporating its October 28, 2021 reports on Apple’s consolidated financial statements and internal control over financial reporting into seven specified Apple registration statements. CEO Timothy Cook and CFO Luca Maestri certify that they reviewed Apple’s fiscal 2021 Form 10-K, that its disclosures are not materially misleading and its financial information fairly presents results and condition, and that they oversee and evaluated disclosure and financial-reporting controls, reported material control changes, and disclosed significant deficiencies, weaknesses, and relevant fraud to auditors and the audit committee. Both certifications are dated October 28, 2021.

title: CERTIFICATIONS OF CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER AND CHIEF FINANCIAL OFFICER PURSUANT TO 18 U.S.C. SECTION 1350, AS ADOPTED PURSUANT TO SECTION 906 OF THE SARBANES-OXLEY ACT OF 2002
summary: Apple CEO Timothy D. Cook and CFO Luca Maestri each certify under Section 906 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act that Apple’s 2021 Form 10-K complies with applicable Securities Exchange Act reporting requirements and fairly presents the company’s financial condition and operating results. Both certifications are dated October 28, 2021. Apple retains the signed original and will provide it to the SEC or its staff upon request.
